doc.title: Ray Conniff interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998

title: Mitch Miller gives Conniff his first break
summary: Conniff met Miller during the James years, returned to New York, and got a call to arrange for Eileen Rogers; he also studied conducting during the lean years.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Let me ask you a kind of a business question. As you became a well known arranger and producer and so forth, were you able to get better business arrangements with your record company? Did you kind of hold more power in the structure of things?
Well you must have had an arrangement like with Columbia, did you get a percentage of the recording? Were you on contract?

Oh I started out like all the rest of the artists. The first break I got was through Mitch Miller. I met Mitch when I was writing for Harry James’ band, and he would come out to the west coast, and sit in the booth and oversee the sessions. And when I first went back to New York, this is let’s say five or six years later, after I’d been doing arranging for Harry James, I went back — I’d been on the west coast for a while and I decided gee I used to do, I was doing well, but I thought I could be doing better. It seemed like I’m not quite fulfilling what I could really do. And I came in as a trombonist on a record session and Mitch was in the booth on the session. And he came out and said, “hey, Ray, what

you doing in New York?” And I said, “well I’m in town now,” and you know we used to talk about my ideas that I was telling you about, writing commercially for the people about when they fell in love and the time period and the predominance of the rhythm. I said, “you know if you need any arranging done, I’m here, available now,” and he says, “fine, I’ll keep you in mind“ the old line you know — don’t call us we’ll call you. And I thought oh the same old thing. But sure enough, two weeks later he called me, and he got me in to do backings for a girl called Eileen Rogers. And by the way, while I was out in California, during the lean years, I forgot to tell you about this, you know I told you about the lean years? I went out and at the suggestion of Frank DeVol, I bought a book called The Grammar of Conducting. Did you ever see that book? You buy yourself a mirror and you put it up on the wall and you get the music stand, and you picture the full orchestra, all 60 of them, and you conduct “Romeo and Juliet” and you cue everything you know, and you do the whole thing, and you learn you don’t conduct like this. And you keep time, this is a one, and most guys that don’t do it, they just lead like this all the time. But anyway so I studied The Grammar of Conducting, and I started taking piano lessons, which I never did overcome, I never became accomplished on the keyboard. And I would practice the trombone, and I would write. And so anyway, so now it’s coming together. So he called me in about an Eileen Rogers, two sides. And he said to me at the close of the interview, she was there, I got her key you know. I can remember the two songs, it was “Now is the Time,” and “Just a Little Bit More.” That’s how vivid this whole thing is in my mind. And he said as I’m going out the door he said, “by the way, why don’t you write yourself a couple of trombone parts if you want to make yourself a couple extra bucks.” And as I tell you this story, what I’m going to tell you now, took place in about ten seconds. It takes a long time to tell it, but it took place back and forth, a little exchange. The first exchange was, “why don’t you write yourself a couple of trombone parts if you want to make yourself a couple of extra bucks.” And I says, “well who’s conducting?” And this, if you knew me in those days, I’m such an introvert. For me to ask a question like this, God must have been looking over me. I don’t know how I ever asked that question. And he said, “well I’ve got a conductor.” It was a split session. You know how they’d put four songs in on a side, and one artist would do two songs, and another would do two songs. Don Cherry was doing two songs, and Eileen Rogers, my artist was doing two songs. So what he’s telling me is, “I’ve got a conductor hired, Norm Layton is going to be conducting” for Don Cherry, you know, it’s a split session. And I asked the question. So this is the way it went. So he says, “Write yourself a couple of trombone parts.” “Well who’s going to conduct?” And he said, “why would you like to conduct?” And I said, “well yeah.” He said okay.
